title: Replication Fails With Event ID 2042 (Tombstone Lifetime Exceeded)
summary: A DC has not inbound-replicated with a partner for longer than the tombstone lifetime; walk the decision tree from 'is this fixable' to 'this DC must be rebuilt.'
warning_banner: The remediation for a confirmed tombstone-lifetime-exceeded DC is destructive to that DC (forced AD DS removal and metadata cleanup, or full rebuild) - never attempted on a DC that might still hold unreplicated, wanted data without first ruling that out.
symptom: repadmin /showrepl on DC-B reports Event ID 2042: 'The time since last replication with this server has exceeded the tombstone lifetime,' naming DC-A as the source partner.
scope: Limited to the replication relationship between DC-B and DC-A initially, but if DC-B has been isolated this long, every partition it holds is suspect, not just the one partner relationship.
impact: DC-B cannot safely resume replication with DC-A - AD DS blocks it to avoid reintroducing already-garbage-collected deleted objects (lingering objects). Left unresolved, DC-B silently drifts further from the rest of the forest.
evidence: repadmin /showrepl output showing Last Success far older than the tombstone lifetime (default 180 days); Directory Service event log Event ID 2042 on the receiving DC.
likely_causes: DC-B was offline (powered off, disconnected, or in a failed state) for longer than the tombstone lifetime.
A firewall or network change silently blocked replication traffic between DC-B and all its partners for an extended period without alerting.
DC-B is a forgotten/orphaned server object left over from a decommission that was never completed.
diagnostics: Confirm the exact outage duration: check DC-B's last boot time, and cross-reference monitoring/ticket history for when it went unreachable.
Run repadmin /showrepl against every partner DC-B has, not just DC-A, to see if this is a single-link problem or DC-B-wide.
Check whether DC-B is still needed at all - is it a live production DC or a leftover that should have been decommissioned?
decision_points: If DC-B's outage is confirmed to exceed the tombstone lifetime on every partition and every partner: DC-B cannot be safely reconnected as-is - proceed to remediation, do not attempt to force replication.
If DC-B is a leftover/orphaned server that's no longer needed: skip straight to metadata cleanup rather than attempting any recovery.
fix: Per Microsoft's documented approach: disconnect DC-B from the production network, then either forcefully remove AD DS from it (in DSRM if normal removal fails) and clean up its server metadata from the rest of the forest, or reinstall the OS and rebuild it as a fresh DC. Do not re-enable networking on DC-B in its old state before this is done.
validation: After metadata cleanup, confirm DC-B no longer appears in repadmin /showrepl output or Active Directory Sites and Services on any surviving DC, and that NTDS Settings objects for it are gone.
prevention: Alert on DCs with no successful inbound replication for a threshold well under the tombstone lifetime (e.g. 7-14 days) so this is caught and fixed long before it becomes unrecoverable; formally decommission DCs that are being retired instead of just powering them off.

title: A FSMO Role Holder Is Permanently Gone - Seize or Wait?
summary: The DC holding the PDC Emulator role has suffered unrecoverable hardware failure. Decide whether to seize the role and execute it safely.
warning_banner: Seizing a FSMO role is a one-way operation for the old holder: it must NEVER be brought back online afterward while still believing it holds that role, or the forest ends up with two DCs acting as the same single-master authority. Confirm total, permanent unavailability before seizing - if there is any chance the original holder returns, isolate it or wipe it first.
symptom: PDC Emulator-holding DC suffered a motherboard failure with no viable recovery path; password/lockout processing and default GPO application are degraded across the domain.
scope: Domain-wide (PDC Emulator is a per-domain role) - affects password change propagation, account lockout processing, and the domain's authoritative time source if this is the forest root domain.
impact: Users experience delayed password-change propagation and inconsistent lockout status until the role is restored on a healthy DC; if this is the forest-root domain, forest-wide time sync is degraded.
evidence: netdom query fsmo or Get-ADDomain confirms the dead server as the listed PDC Emulator; the server is confirmed unreachable and unrecoverable (hardware vendor/ops confirms no rebuild path).
likely_causes: Accidental deletion of the DC's VM without a pre-transfer of its roles.
Ransomware/compromise requiring the DC to be wiped rather than trusted back online.
diagnostics: Verify via at least two methods (netdom query fsmo and Get-ADDomain/Get-ADForest) that this DC genuinely holds the role and is genuinely unreachable, not just slow to respond.
Confirm with infrastructure/hardware teams that there is no realistic path to bring the original server back online in its current state.
Identify a healthy, well-connected DC in the same domain to receive the seized role.
decision_points: If any realistic path exists to recover the original DC intact: wait and transfer gracefully once it's back, rather than seizing.
If recovery is confirmed impossible (this scenario): seize now rather than leaving the domain running without a PDC Emulator, since delay compounds user-facing impact.
fix: Use ntdsutil (or the equivalent PowerShell seize workflow) to seize the PDC Emulator role onto the chosen healthy DC. Immediately afterward, ensure the dead DC's computer/server object and metadata are cleaned up from AD DS so it can never be mistaken for a live replication partner.
validation: Confirm via netdom query fsmo that the new DC holds the role; test a password change and confirm it processes normally; if forest-root, confirm time sync (w32tm /monitor) is now anchored correctly.
prevention: Maintain a documented, pre-agreed standby FSMO holder per role (per Microsoft's placement guidance) so a seize decision under incident pressure has a pre-vetted target rather than an improvised one; ensure backups exist for all role-holding DCs specifically.

title: Multiple DCs Failing Simultaneously - Is This Forest Recovery Territory?
summary: Several DCs across domains stop replicating and show directory corruption symptoms at once. Decide whether this is a multi-DC outage or a genuine forest-wide failure requiring the recovery guide.
warning_banner: Do not initiate forest recovery procedures (authoritative restores, forced DC removal at scale) until forest-wide failure is actually confirmed - misclassifying a smaller, contained incident as a forest-wide failure and starting recovery procedures unnecessarily makes the outage worse.
symptom: Three of eight DCs across two domains stop accepting logons and show directory database errors within the same hour; the remaining five DCs appear healthy so far.
scope: Potentially forest-wide if the cause is a spreading corruption, malicious schema change, or compromised credential reused across DCs; potentially contained if the three affected DCs share a specific, isolated fault (same storage array, same recent patch batch).
impact: If misclassified as contained when it is actually forest-wide: recovery is delayed while corruption or compromise continues to spread. If misclassified as forest-wide when it is actually contained: unnecessary forest-wide recovery destroys more recent data than needed and causes far more downtime than the incident required.
evidence: Event logs on affected DCs (schema changes, corruption errors, unexpected AD DS service crashes); a timeline of exactly which DCs failed and when; whether the failures share an infrastructure root cause (same physical host, same SAN, same recent patch) versus none.
likely_causes: Shared underlying infrastructure fault (e.g. all three DCs are VMs on the same failed storage array) - contained, not forest-wide.
An attacker or accidental script executing a destructive or schema-altering change that is actively replicating outward - genuinely forest-wide and time-critical.
A bad patch or update pushed simultaneously to a subset of DCs - contained to that patch ring.
diagnostics: Work with the platform/hosting team to check for a shared infrastructure root cause across exactly the affected DCs first - this is the fastest way to rule out 'forest-wide.'
Check whether any schema or configuration-partition changes occurred forest-wide around the incident start time (these replicate everywhere and are a strong forest-wide signal).
Assess whether unaffected DCs can still process authentication and updates normally - if yes, the failure is not yet forest-wide even if it could become so.
decision_points: Shared, isolated infrastructure cause with unaffected DCs still healthy: contained incident - recover the affected DCs individually (rebuild/restore just those three), no full forest recovery needed.

Evidence of an actively spreading malicious or corrupting change, or genuine inability of any DC in the forest to process changes: treat as forest-wide - escalate to the full forest recovery guide and involve Microsoft Support and business stakeholders per the guide's 'identify the problem' phase before touching backups.
fix: For the contained case: individually rebuild or restore the three affected DCs from backup/redeploy while leaving the healthy five untouched, then verify replication converges normally. For the confirmed forest-wide case: follow the forest recovery guide's five phases in order, starting with the forest root domain.
validation: Contained case: confirm all eight DCs show 0 replication failures and consistent directory content afterward. Forest-wide case: validate per the forest recovery lab's own validation steps (OSB-AD-LAB-0003) before reconnecting anything to production.
prevention: Maintain infrastructure diversity for DCs (avoid single points of shared failure like one storage array hosting all DCs in a domain); monitor for unexpected schema/configuration-partition changes as a distinct, high-priority alert separate from routine replication monitoring.

title: Service Access Fails With KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED
summary: A specific service intermittently fails Kerberos authentication with KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED; work through the SPN-uniqueness and clock-skew branches.
symptom: Users intermittently fail to access a web application with an authentication error; event logs on the target server show Event ID 4, KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED.
scope: Limited to the specific service/SPN combination reported, but if the SPN is duplicated it may affect any client trying to reach that service from anywhere in the forest.
impact: Intermittent, hard-to-reproduce authentication failures for the affected application, which is often mistaken for an application bug rather than an AD issue.
evidence: Event ID 4 (KRB_AP_ERR_MODIFIED) on the target server's Security/System log; the error means the client couldn't decrypt the service ticket, which per Microsoft's guidance points to clock skew or a non-unique SPN as the two leading causes.
likely_causes: The service's SPN is registered on more than one account in the forest (e.g. both the service's dedicated service account and a decommissioned test account still hold it).
Client and target server clocks have drifted beyond the Kerberos tolerance.
In a multi-domain forest, the service account name isn't unique across trusted domains.
diagnostics: Search the forest for duplicate SPN registrations: setspn -X (or equivalent Get-ADObject -LDAPFilter query) to find any SPN registered on more than one object.
Check w32tm status on both the client and the target server to confirm they're within the default 5-minute Kerberos clock tolerance of the domain hierarchy's time source.
Run klist tickets on an affected client immediately after a failure to inspect which service ticket was involved.
decision_points: If setspn -X finds a duplicate: remove the SPN from whichever account should not hold it (usually the decommissioned/incorrect one) - do this first since it's the most common cause of this exact error.
If no duplicate SPN is found but clocks are out of sync: fix time sync instead; don't touch SPN registrations that are actually correct.
fix: Remove the duplicate SPN registration from the incorrect account with setspn -D <SPN> <WrongAccount>, or correct time sync with w32tm /resync /rediscover on the drifting system(s), depending on which diagnostic pointed to the actual cause.
validation: Have an affected user retry access immediately after the fix and confirm success; re-run setspn -X to confirm no duplicates remain forest-wide, not just for this one service.
prevention: Decommission service accounts and their SPNs together, never leave an orphaned SPN behind on a retired account; monitor domain-wide time sync health as a standing check, not just during incidents.

title: A New Host Can't Retrieve Its gMSA Password
summary: Test-ADServiceAccount returns False on a newly added farm member; work through the authorization-list and encryption-type branches.
symptom: A newly provisioned server added to an existing gMSA-backed service farm fails to start the service; Test-ADServiceAccount on the new host returns False.
scope: Limited to the newly added host; existing farm members continue working normally, confirming the gMSA itself is healthy.
impact: The new host cannot join the service farm until resolved, reducing farm capacity/redundancy versus plan.
evidence: Test-ADServiceAccount -Identity <gmsa> returns False on the new host but True on existing farm members; the gMSA account object itself shows no errors.
likely_causes: The new host's computer account was never added to the gMSA's PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword list - the single most common cause.
The new host is configured to reject RC4 but the gMSA account's msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes attribute isn't set to include AES.
The new host hasn't rebooted/re-authenticated since being added to the correct security group backing the gMSA's authorization.
diagnostics: Run Get-ADServiceAccount -Identity <gmsa> -Properties PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword and check whether the new host's computer account (or its group) is actually listed.
If using a group for authorization, confirm the new host's computer account is actually a member and that group membership has replicated to the DC the host is contacting.
Check the new host's configured Kerberos encryption types against the gMSA account's msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes attribute.
decision_points: Host/group missing from the authorization list: fix the authorization list - this resolves the large majority of these cases.
Authorization is correct but encryption types mismatch: fix msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes on the gMSA account or the host's encryption policy instead.
fix: Add the new host (or its group) to the gMSA's authorized list: Set-ADServiceAccount -Identity <gmsa> -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword <hosts-or-group>, then on the new host run Install-ADServiceAccount -Identity <gmsa> again and re-test.
validation: Test-ADServiceAccount -Identity <gmsa> returns True on the new host; the service starts successfully using the gMSA identity.
prevention: Use a dedicated AD security group (not individual host entries) as PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword for any farm expected to scale, so adding a new host only requires a group membership change, not a gMSA object edit.
